p: Jordan Reyes has never flown anything.
Her older brother Danny died in March, at his daughter's soccer game.
For eleven years he flew a white 1978 Cessna called Biscuit out of Centennial Airport, south of Denver, and owned a quarter of her with three partners in a little flying club.
The book opens on the day his will is read.
Abby quotes the FAA's books by their initials. The PHAK is the pilot's handbook, the AFH is the flying handbook, the AIM is the procedures manual, and the ACS is the standard the checkride grades.
The people you'll hear from first.
Claire Reyes. Danny's widow. She's a nurse in a Denver emergency room.
Walt Herrera. One of Danny's three partners, a retired airline dispatcher.
Russ Kim. Another partner, usually out of town for work and posting in the club's group chat.
Abby Strand. The club's flight instructor.
Danny Reyes. Jordan's brother. You'll hear him in his own words.
Lourdes Reyes. Jordan and Danny's mother.
The lawyer read the will in a conference room that smelled like carpet glue, and the part about the airplane took eleven seconds.

Last will of Daniel A. Reyes, article six. To my sister Jordan, my one quarter share in the Hangar Six Flying Club and the aircraft N4791E, with my logbook and my headset if Marisol can find it. Learn to fly it or sell it to Walt. Don't let it sit.

Claire laughed once, the short tired laugh she'd been using since March, and then put her hand over her mouth. Their mother looked at the table. Jordan looked at the sentence until it stopped being words.

Danny had been forty one. He'd collapsed on the sideline of an under ten soccer game in Parker on a bright Saturday morning, cheering for Ellie, and he'd been gone before the ambulance got out of the parking lot. Sudden cardiac arrest, the doctor said, the kind nobody sees coming, the kind that has nothing to do with anything you did. The airplane had nothing to do with it either. Jordan kept having to remind people of that, and then kept having to remind herself. She'd worked more cardiac arrests than she could count. She knew exactly what the crew had done on that sideline, and that they'd done it right, and that it hadn't mattered.

Jordan was thirty five. She was a paramedic in Aurora, twenty four hours on and forty eight off, which meant she walked into strangers' worst days and worked the problem in order. Airway, breathing, circulation. She was good at it. She was the one who stayed calm and did the sensible thing. Danny was the one who called from Moab at midnight to say he'd landed on a dirt strip and you should've seen it.
In the parking lot after the reading, her phone buzzed. A number she didn't have saved.

A text from Walt Herrera. Jordan, this is Walt Herrera from Hangar Six. I'm sorry about your brother. He was a good man and a better partner. I'll be straight with you because Danny would want that. The club agreement gives you a year. I'll buy the share back at book value today if you want, no hard feelings. Call me when you're ready.

Jordan read it twice. Then she did something she could only explain later as stubbornness. She searched "discovery flight Centennial Airport," found a club page with a photo of a white and maroon Cessna she'd seen in a hundred of Danny's texts, and booked the first open Saturday with an instructor named Abby Strand.
She told herself she was doing it so she could say no with a clear conscience. You can't turn something down properly if you've never looked at it.
Abby's Ground School: what you're signing up for.
The road to a private pilot certificate.

Welcome to the briefing room. It's a folding table, a whiteboard, and a coffee maker older than I am. Here's the whole thing in one picture. I'm drawing a line across the board with a box at each end. Left box, you. Right box, private pilot. Everything in between is paperwork, money, and about sixty hours of being wrong in an airplane.

The first piece is the student pilot certificate. You apply through the FAA's online system, IACRA, usually with me sitting next to you, and the certificate comes in the mail a few weeks later. You need to be at least 16 to get one for airplanes and able to read, speak, write, and understand English. You can take lessons before it arrives. You can't fly solo without it.

The second piece is the medical certificate. To fly solo, a student pilot needs at least a third class medical, issued by an aviation medical examiner, called an AME, after you fill out the application online in MedXPress. A third class medical is the usual way to use private pilot privileges. If you're under 40 on the day of the exam, it's good through the last day of the 60th month after the month of the exam. At 40 or older, the 24th month. Get the medical first. Before you spend three thousand dollars. If anything in your history needs a closer look, you want to know now.

To be eligible for the private certificate itself, 14 CFR 61.103 says you must be at least 17, meet the English requirement, pass the knowledge test, pass the practical test, called the checkride, and meet the experience requirements. Those are in 61.109: at least 40 hours of flight time, including at least 20 hours of flight training from an authorized instructor and at least 10 hours of solo flight. Inside those numbers sit specific requirements. With an instructor: 3 hours of cross country, 3 hours of night, 3 hours of flying by instruments, and 3 hours of checkride prep within the preceding 2 calendar months. The night training includes one night cross country over 100 nautical miles total and 10 night takeoffs and full stop landings. Solo: 5 hours of cross country, including one trip of at least 150 nautical miles total, with full stop landings at three points and one leg of at least 50 nautical miles. Last, 3 solo takeoffs and full stop landings at an airport with an operating control tower.

Forty is a legal minimum, not a prediction. Most people take more. Nobody gets a prize for forty. Schools that train under Part 141 have an FAA approved syllabus and a 35 hour minimum. Clubs and independent instructors like me train under Part 61. Either way you take the same knowledge test and the same checkride.

How the exam asks it. Memorize 61.103 and 61.109. The test loves the numbers: 17 years old, 40 hours total, 20 dual, 10 solo, 150 nautical miles with three landings and one 50 mile leg, and 3 full stop landings at a towered field.

Here's an airplane. Yes, it looks like a fish. Now four arrows. Lift points up, perpendicular to the relative wind. Weight points down, toward the center of the earth. Thrust points forward, from the propeller. Drag points back, opposing motion through the air. In steady, unaccelerated flight, the forces are in balance: the sum of the upward forces equals the sum of the downward forces, and the sum of the forward forces equals the sum of the rearward forces. Change one, and the airplane accelerates, climbs, or descends until a new balance arrives.

One more word while the fish is up there. The relative wind is the air flowing past the wing, opposite the airplane's flight path, so it comes from wherever you're going, not from the weather. The angle between that and the chord line, an imaginary straight line from the wing's leading edge to its trailing edge, is the angle of attack. Pull back and you raise it. Raise it too far and the wing quits, at any speed. We'll come back to that in October.
Pilots spend their whole lives managing these four. More power, more thrust. Pull back, more lift for a moment, then more drag. Every bag you throw in the back is weight. You'll see.

Someday at 3,000 feet I'm going to pull the power and ask you what's left of the four forces. So, the engine quits. Thrust is gone, but lift and weight and drag are all still there, so the airplane doesn't fall out of the sky. It glides, trading height for speed like a bike coasting downhill with your feet off the pedals. So the first move after an engine failure is the same every single time: pitch for best glide and trim for it. In Biscuit that's 65 knots. Best glide is the speed that carries you the farthest for the altitude you've got. Faster, you come down faster. Slower, you come down a little slower but cover less ground, and down near minimum sink you stay up longest and get the least distance. Then you pick a field. Then, and only then, the emergency checklist: fuel selector, mixture, carb heat, mags. Airplane, field, checklist. In that order. I'll show you before we land today.
How the exam asks it. Watch the wording. In straight and level unaccelerated flight the opposing forces are equal. "Lift is greater than weight" describes a climb starting, not a steady climb.

Biscuit has the five main parts every airplane has. The fuselage holds the people, the cargo, and the controls. The wings make lift; Biscuit's are mounted high and braced by struts. The empennage is the tail: the vertical stabilizer with the rudder hinged to it, and the horizontal stabilizer with the elevator hinged to it, and a small trim tab on the elevator. The landing gear on a 172 is fixed tricycle gear, a nose wheel and two mains. The powerplant is the engine and propeller, in Biscuit's case a carbureted four cylinder Lycoming with 160 horsepower.

Inside, Biscuit has the six gauges every trainer her age has, two rows of three. Top row: airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter. Bottom row: turn coordinator, heading indicator, vertical speed indicator. Pilots call it the six pack. The attitude indicator is the one with the little orange airplane over a ball that's blue on top and brown on the bottom. It's a picture of the horizon, and it's the one you lean on when you can't see the real one. The altimeter tells you how high you are above sea level, not above the ground. At an airport that already sits at 5,885 feet, that difference is the whole ballgame.
How the exam asks it. Expect a figure of an airplane with parts labeled by number. Know where the elevator, rudder, ailerons, flaps, and trim tab live.
Three axes and the controls that move them.

An airplane rotates around three axes, and all three pass through the center of gravity. The longitudinal axis runs nose to tail; rotation around it is roll, controlled by the ailerons. The lateral axis runs wingtip to wingtip; rotation around it is pitch, controlled by the elevator. The vertical axis runs top to bottom; rotation around it is yaw, controlled by the rudder.

Turn the yoke left and the left aileron goes up while the right aileron goes down. The wing with the lowered aileron makes more lift, and it also makes more induced drag, which pulls the nose the wrong way, away from the turn. That's adverse yaw. You fix it by pressing the rudder pedal on the same side as the turn. That's coordinated flight, and the ball in the turn coordinator tells you whether you've got it. Step on the ball. You'll hear me say that four hundred times.

The elevator trim tab relieves control pressure so you don't have to hold the yoke forward or back the whole flight. It moves opposite the elevator: to hold the nose down, the tab moves up, which pushes the elevator down. In Biscuit you turn a wheel between the seats. Fly the attitude you want, then trim until your hands can relax.

How the exam asks it. Two classics: which axis does each control move (ailerons and roll, elevator and pitch, rudder and yaw), and which way the airplane yaws when you roll with ailerons alone (away from the turn).
Who's in charge, and what you check first.

Two regulations you'll hear me quote before you ever touch the throttle. 91.3 says the pilot in command is directly responsible for the flight and is the final authority on it. Not the instructor in the right seat once you're certificated, not the passenger who's late for dinner, not the guy in the group chat. In an emergency that needs action right now, 91.3 lets you deviate from any rule in Part 91 as far as the emergency requires. If you do, the FAA can ask you for a written report afterward, and you send one.

91.103 is preflight action, and it's the reason I make you read things. Before every flight you have to become familiar with all available information about it. For any flight, that means the runway lengths where you'll take off and land, and the takeoff and landing distance data for your airplane. For a flight that leaves the area around the airport, it also means the weather reports and forecasts, your fuel requirements, the alternatives if you can't finish the flight as planned, and any traffic delays ATC has told you about. All available information. That's a big phrase, and the test likes it.

The first thing you check isn't the airplane. It's you. Pilots run a checklist on themselves called IMSAFE: illness, medication, stress, alcohol, fatigue, emotion. Is anything on that list going to make you worse at this today? Stress and fatigue are the two people lie about, because you can still walk and talk and make coffee. Judgment goes first, and you're the last one to notice it went. Alcohol has a hard rule, 91.17: nothing to drink within eight hours of flying, under 0.04 percent blood alcohol, never while you're under the influence, and no drug that dulls you. Eight hours bottle to throttle is the floor, not the plan. If you answer any letter with a yes, tell me, and we'll decide together whether today's the day.

Then the airplane. The preflight inspection is a walkaround with the checklist in your hand, in the same order every time. Biscuit's starts inside: master on to check the fuel gauges and the lights, master off, key out, key on the glare shield where everybody can see it. Outside, you check fuel quantity with your eyes and a dipstick, not with the gauges. You drain a fuel sample from each wing and from the strainer and look at it. Blue means 100LL. Water sinks to the bottom of the cup in little beads. You check the oil level on the dipstick. You move every control surface by hand and look at the hinges, the bolts, and the cotter pins. Tires, brake lines, the pitot tube with its cover off, the static port, the fuel vent. And inside again, the fuel selector on BOTH. Biscuit's is sticky.

Every item is there because of something that happened to somebody. Water in the fuel quits engines on takeoff, so you sample. A control surface that's loose or jammed is a loss of control, so you move them all. And while you walk you're hunting defects. Cracks, especially near hinges and at the edges of the cowling. Leaks: oil dripping under the engine, blue fuel stains on the wing where the fuel dye dried. Loose rivets, which sometimes leave a dark ring of aluminum dust around the head. Mechanics call that a smoking rivet. Corrosion. Nicks on the front edge of the propeller, because a nick concentrates stress and grows into a crack. Find something you can't name, and we don't fly until Marisol names it.

A word about checklists, since people use them two ways. A read-and-do list is just what it sounds like. Read an item, do it, read the next. That's how you'll use them while you're learning. Later some of it becomes a flow you do from memory and then check against the card, flow then verify. Either way the list gets read. Look at the windsock on the walk out. And latch both doors, the handle and the little latch at the top, because Biscuit's right door pops open on rotation if you skip the top one.
How the exam asks it. Know who has final authority, what 91.3 allows in an emergency, and the 91.103 list for a flight not in the vicinity of an airport.

A discovery flight with a certificated flight instructor is real flight training, and it can be logged as dual instruction received toward 61.109. You keep your own logbook, in your own name. I write the entry and sign it. Buy the logbook. It's twelve bucks, and it's the only thing in aviation that is.
How the exam asks it. Training time from an authorized instructor counts toward the minimums when it's logged and signed. The pilot keeps the record; the instructor endorses it.
Tuesday night, alone in the station day room after the rest of the crew went to bed, Jordan did what she always did with a call she didn't understand. She took it apart.

She wiped the whiteboard and wrote PRIVATE PILOT at the top, then a column of everything she'd read in two hours of FAA websites, forum arguments, and a YouTube video of a man eating a sandwich while explaining airspace. One year on Walt's clock. Danny had done it in seven months, while working, which Jordan knew because Danny had told her about forty times.
She had to decide what went first. What does Jordan put at the top of the plan?
A. Book lessons now and get the medical once she's close to her first solo.
B. Plan on BasicMed, like a lot of club pilots, and skip the AME exam.
C. Budget for the 40 hour minimum in 61.109 and book lessons to match.
D. Book the AME exam first, before she spends a dollar on flight lessons.

She circles MEDICAL and writes "first, before money." Under it: student certificate through IACRA with the instructor, then the 61.109 list, then a budget with a fat margin. It looks like a protocol card. That makes her feel better than it should.

That's it. Medical first, because it's the only item that can end the whole thing, and you want to know before you've spent anything. Then the student certificate, so you're ready to solo when you're ready. Then budget for reality, not the minimum.
Abby called on Wednesday to confirm Saturday. She talked fast, like someone who billed in tenths of an hour.
Do you have a medical yet? Doesn't matter for Saturday. Matters for everything after.
Jordan had the MedXPress page open in another tab. There were three classes, and the form wanted to know which one.
Under 14 CFR Part 61, what medical certificate fits Jordan's goal?
A. A first class medical, the top class, good for any flying she might do later.
B. A second class medical, the one that lets her carry paying passengers.
C. No medical yet. A student pilot can wait until just before the checkride.
D. A third class medical, the one that private pilot privileges call for.

Third class. That's the one for private pilots. Good. You're thirty five, so it's good for 60 calendar months. Book the AME this week. Tell me what they say. Jordan books one in Englewood for the following Thursday.
Yep. That's the one. Private pilots need a third class. You're under 40 at the exam, so it lasts through the end of the 60th month after the month of the exam. Book it early, before you're invested.
Russ Kim, the partner Jordan had never met, added her to the club group chat on Thursday. The first message was a welcome. The second was advice nobody asked for.

A message from Russ Kim. welcome jordan. sorry about danny, he was the best of us. unsolicited tip: abby's great but she's leaving for the airlines eventually, they all do. the 141 school at the north end has a 35 hr minimum. just saying
Jordan had read about Part 141 too. She'd also read Abby's bio, which said she was at 1,040 hours and counting.
Russ says the club's instructor will leave for the airlines, like they all do. What should Jordan do?
A. Track down the instructor who trained Danny and ask to learn from them.
B. Ask Abby straight out what happens to her students when she leaves.
C. Sign up with the Part 141 school at the north end and its 35 hour syllabus.
D. Call around to other instructors in the area and go with the lowest rate.

Russ says you'll leave for the airlines. When, and what happens to your students when you do? Abby doesn't blink. Probably a year. When I go, you get a handoff, my notes, and a CFI I trust. I'll put that in writing if you want. Jordan doesn't need it in writing. She likes that Abby offered.

Exactly right. Choosing an instructor is choosing a person. Ask the hard question early: availability, schedule, what happens if they leave. A good instructor has a plan for continuity and isn't offended that you asked.
Decision four. Anything I should know.
Saturday came in clear and cold. Centennial sat at the south edge of the city, flat and wide, with the mountains standing up along the whole west side like a wall someone forgot to finish.

Abby met her in the club office with a clipboard and a cup of coffee she didn't offer to share. She was shorter than Jordan had pictured, with a pencil behind her ear and the expression of someone running numbers.
Before we go out. Anything I should know? Sleep, meds, sick, anything. I ask everybody.
Jordan had slept about four hours. She'd been sleeping about four hours since March.
Abby asks everyone the same fitness question before a flight. How should Jordan answer?
A. Tell Abby she's fine, and save the rest for after the flight.
B. Tell Abby her brother died in March and she's barely sleeping.
C. Tell Abby she's a little short on sleep and leave it at that.
D. Cancel the flight and rebook for once she's sleeping better.

About four hours. My brother died in March. He was one of the partners here. Abby is quiet for a second. Danny. She doesn't make it a question. Okay. We keep it short and easy. You say stop, we stop. No speech. Jordan's grateful for the no speech.

That's it. IMSAFE: illness, medication, stress, alcohol, fatigue, emotion. Grief is stress, fatigue, and emotion at once. Saying it out loud lets the pilot in command plan around it. That's how risk management starts.

Biscuit sat on the ramp in a row of tied down Cessnas, white with a maroon stripe, a little faded. Jordan knew her from Danny's photos, always with his thumb in the corner. In person she was smaller. She looked like a used car somebody loved.
Abby handed her a laminated checklist, worn soft at the corners, with a coffee ring on the back. You do the walkaround. I'll follow you and keep my mouth shut. Mostly.
Jordan has the club's worn checklist and her first preflight inspection ahead. How should she do it?
A. Work down the checklist line by line, asking Abby about anything new.
B. Follow the checklist, skipping the items she doesn't understand for Abby to cover.
C. Watch Abby do this first walkaround, then do the next one herself.
D. Do it from memory, the way the pilot did it in the video she watched last night.

It takes twenty five minutes. She asks about the stall warning horn, the static port, and why the pitot tube has a cover on it. Abby answers every one. At the end she says, You read the whole thing. Most people read the bold parts.
Yep. That's the one. Read and do, one item at a time, and ask about what you don't know. A preflight inspection is where you find what will hurt you later on the ground, where it's cheap.
Decision six. The bead in the cup.
Under the left wing, Abby handed her a clear plastic tube with a pin on the end. Fuel sample. Push it up into the drain, fill the cup, look at it.
The fuel was pale blue, the color of a swimming pool in a commercial. At the bottom of the cup sat a small clear bead that didn't mix, like a drop of oil in reverse.
What should Jordan do about what she found in the fuel sample?
A. Treat it as a single drop and finish the rest of the walkaround.
B. Finish the walkaround, then tell Abby before they get in.
C. Pour the sample back in through the filler cap and keep going.
D. Show Abby, and keep draining until the samples come out clean.
She drains three more cups. The third is clear and blue all the way down. Abby nods. Cold night, partly full tank, condensation. That's why we look every single time.

Exactly right. Water's heavier than gas. It sinks, so the sump catches it first. You drain until it's blue top to bottom with no junk in it. Won't clear? Then we're not going, and I'm calling Marisol.

Abby put her in the left seat like it was nothing. It wasn't nothing. Danny's seat. Jordan ran a hand over the panel: six round gauges, a radio stack, a GPS bolted in sometime this century, a crack in the glare shield held together with silver tape. A sticker by the mag switch said HI DAD in a little kid's handwriting. She looked at it a while.
Down on the floor between the seats was the fuel selector, a red handle. The checklist said: Fuel selector valve, BOTH. She turned it. It stuck a few degrees short of the click and wouldn't go.
What should Jordan do when a checklist item doesn't go as written before engine start?
A. Force it into the detent herself rather than look nervous.
B. Leave it a few degrees short, close to the BOTH detent.
C. Tell Abby it won't seat, and ask her to check it.
D. Set it to LEFT, a position it turns to freely.

Ah. Biscuit's famous selector. She shows her the trick, lift and twist, and it clicks home. Marisol knows. It's on the squawk list. It's safe, it's just ornery. Good catch, though. You'll always feel for the click.
That's it. Something feels off, you say so, and you say it before we start the engine. Takeoff and landing in this airplane are on BOTH. Ten seconds of asking beats a very bad afternoon.

They took off on runway three five right behind a Cirrus. Biscuit's door popped open with a bang at rotation, which Abby had warned her about and which still nearly stopped her heart. Abby latched the top and said, Biscuit does that. Danny never fixed it. Said it kept him humble. It was the first time anyone had said Danny's name like it was normal.

East of the airport the city gave up and the plains took over, brown squares and a few center pivots and a feedlot you could smell at altitude, honestly. Abby kept tapping the chart on her knee where the Class B shelf sat over their heads like a low ceiling. Then she let go of the yoke. Yours. Roll left. Just your hands. Feet flat. Watch the nose, not me.
She rolled. The nose did a little shrug to the right, wrong way, then came around. See that? Why'd it do that? The yoke was cold under her fingers.
In a left roll with hands only, what makes the nose swing right?
A. The lowered right aileron adds drag on that wing. Left rudder fixes it.
B. Airplanes lag a little. Hold the yoke steady, and give it a second.
C. The left aileron went down, and the extra drag on that side swung the nose right.
D. A gust from the left, the usual lumpy April air over the plains.

The right aileron went down. More drag on that side, so the nose goes right. Abby turns in her seat to look at Jordan. You read the book. Jordan says, I read the book. Okay. Do it again with left rudder. The nose swings straight into the turn. The ball sits in the middle. Abby's kneeboard had a sticker on it that said I'D RATHER BE HOLDING SHORT.

Yep. That's the one. That's adverse yaw. The wing with the lowered aileron makes more lift and more induced drag, and the drag pulls the nose away from the turn. Rudder in the direction of the turn coordinates it.

Okay. Before anything fun, we look around. Every single time. I'll do the first one. Ninety degrees left, ninety back right, her head on a swivel the entire time, chattering about how she once found a hot air balloon this way.
Second turn was Jordan's. Bottom right corner of the windshield, a dot. Two o'clock-ish, below them. She watched it for a full breath waiting for it to drift. It didn't drift. It got bigger.
During clearing turns, Jordan sees an airplane that may be on a collision course. What should she do first?
A. Keep watching it, and let Abby spot it on her own.
B. Point at it and say "Traffic, two o'clock low."
C. Take the yoke and turn away from it herself, right now.
D. Ask Abby whether that dot at two o'clock is a bird.

She points. Traffic, two o'clock low. Abby's head whips around. Got him. Piper Warrior, climbing. My airplane, turning left. Over they go. The Piper passes behind the wing, close enough to read the N number if she'd been looking, which she wasn't, because her heart was in her ears. Nice call. That's the most important thing I'll ever teach you and you did it on day one. Don't get cocky. Jordan's own headset was a loaner with one split ear cushion.

Exactly right. Out here, in good weather, the traffic system is mostly us, looking out the window. So you call it like a clock, plus high or low, and you keep your eyes glued to it. A dot that won't move on the glass but keeps growing? Collision course. Remember that one forever.

Back up to altitude. Five minutes later Jordan's right forearm was on fire. Biscuit wanted up. Jordan wanted level. So she pushed. And pushed. Her watch buzzed to tell her her heart rate was elevated, which, thanks. She did a quick inventory: wrist sore, forearm burning, altimeter creeping, attitude indicator a hair nose high, Abby's coffee untouched on the floor by her boot.
Abby looked at Jordan's arm. Then out the window. Then at the arm. She didn't say anything. Jordan was starting to learn that Abby not saying anything was a kind of saying something.
Jordan is holding Biscuit level by pushing on the yoke. What should she do?
A. Hand it back to Abby for a minute and shake her arm out.
B. Pull a little power and let the nose settle down on its own.
C. Hold the attitude she wants, then trim until the pressure is gone.
D. Keep pushing. She has fifteen more minutes in her, and her arm can take it.

Three turns forward on the wheel. The yoke goes soft in her hand. She lets go, cautiously, like taking her hand off a kid's bike seat, and Biscuit stays put, level, droning along. She laughs. It surprises both of them. Yep. That's trim. Welcome to not arm wrestling your airplane.

That's it. Attitude, then trim. The trim tab rides on the back of the elevator and moves opposite it, which is a test question, write that down. Its whole job is to hold the elevator so your arm doesn't have to.

Last thing, then home. I'm going to show you something. Nothing is wrong with the airplane. Say it back. Nothing is wrong with the airplane. Abby nodded. Great. Carb heat knob, out. Throttle, all the way back to the stop. Out the side window the plains were doing nothing at all, mile after mile of it.

The engine dropped to a mutter. The quiet was enormous. Jordan's stomach dropped with the nose, and for a second the only thing in her head was a Saturday sideline in Parker and a phone call she didn't make in time.
Your airplane, Abby said. The engine just quit. What's the first thing you do?
A. Get the nose down to best glide speed, then go hunting for a field.
B. Key the mic and tell Centennial Tower she's declaring an emergency now.
C. Bank back toward Centennial and head for the nearest runway.
D. Go straight for the key and the mags and get it running again.

Nose down. The needle creeps to the spot Abby's fingernail is tapping on the glass and sits there. Then she looks outside: a long brown field, a dirt road along one side, a windmill, no power lines that she can find. Yep. That's it. That's the whole trick. Throttle in, engine roaring, and Jordan notices she hasn't breathed since Parker.

Yep. That's the one. Fly first. Best glide gets you the most ground for the altitude you've got. Then pick your spot, then the checklist, then the radio. Aviate, navigate, communicate. In that order, every time.

After they tied Biscuit down, a man in a canvas jacket was waiting at the hangar door with two coffees. Gray at the temples, reading glasses on a cord, the posture of somebody who'd spent thirty years telling people things they didn't want to hear. Walt Herrera.

He handed Jordan a coffee. How was it? Then, before Jordan could answer: I meant what I said. I'm not trying to take anything from you. But you've got a lot on you right now, you've never flown, and that's a quarter of an airplane four people trust their lives to. So. Selling?
A. Tell Walt it's her share now and to stay out of it.
B. Sell the share back to keep the peace, and let the airplane go.
C. Show Walt the plan, and ask what he needs to see along the way.
D. Promise Walt she'll solo in three months, like Danny did.

She pulls up the whiteboard photo on her phone: medical first, student certificate, training, a budget with margin. Walt reads it twice with his glasses on. Medical first, he says. Huh. Then: I want to see your logbook every month. And you come to the safety meetings. It isn't a yes. It isn't a no.
Exactly right. Walt's worry is legitimate. Answer it with a plan and checkpoints, not with feelings. Inviting the skeptic to watch your progress turns him from an obstacle into a safety net.
Walt left. Abby went inside to write up the flight. Jordan said she'd be a minute.

She walked back out to the ramp and untied nothing and opened Biscuit's left door, the one that popped, and sat down in the left seat. The cabin smelled like old vinyl and avgas and, faintly, something she couldn't name and then could. Danny's car had smelled like that. She'd thought it was Danny's cologne.

In the side pocket of the door there was a fuel tester, a pencil, half a roll of Tums, and a composition notebook with a cracked green spine. On the cover, in Sharpie: D. REYES. IF FOUND, I'M PROBABLY NEARBY.
It wasn't the official logbook. That was in a box at Claire's house. This was the other one, the one Danny kept in the airplane. She opened it to the first page.

Danny's logbook, first page. March 14. First lesson. 0.9 dual. Cessna 152. Instructor says I'm a natural. Instructor says that to everyone. Did steep turns, almost threw up, didn't. Felt like I was ten years old. Bring Jordan someday. She'll hate it and then she won't.

Jordan read it three times. Then she closed the notebook and put both hands on the yoke and sat there for ten minutes, not flying anywhere, not doing anything, watching a Cirrus taxi out and the light go long and gold across the field toward the mountains.
Abby came out once, saw her through the windshield, and went back inside without a word. She'd thank Abby for that later.
She didn't tell anyone what she did in those ten minutes. She didn't really know.
That night her mother called. She let it ring twice before she answered. Claire said you went to the airport. A pause long enough to fly through. Mija. Please don't do this.
She looked at the green notebook on her kitchen counter. I booked the medical, she said. Thursday. That's all I've done, Ma. That's all I've decided.
It was true. It just didn't feel like the whole truth.
